newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine Chernobyl statements fail to calm opinion.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine Chernobyl statements fail to calm opinion.

text.p: Official attempts to ease public concern over the Chernobyl nuclear power plant appeared to have failed on Thursday as Ukrainian and Russian media speculated on whether the station's ruined reactor could explode again.

Commentators suggested Ukraine was exploiting increased neutron radiation readings inside the "sarcophagus" covering the fourth reactor to secure more Western funds to close the plant -- site of the world's biggest nuclear accident in 1986.
"Is a new explosion brewing under the sarcophagus?" screamed the headline in the daily Vseukrainsky Vedomosti.
"How long can we soldier on like this?" said Demokratychna Ukraina. "'Something is happening under the sarcophagus'. That is the clearest scientific explanation we have been given."
Russia's top liberal daily Izvestia was far blunter.
"Nuclear blackmail for their own ends?" read the daily's headline. "Kiev is again using Chernobyl to intimidate the world but specialists see no real danger."

Ukraine's nuclear authorities launched another attempt to ease the tension unleashed by Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko's statement this week that a limited nuclear chain reaction had occurred inside the "tomb".
The State Nuclear authority, Derzhkomatom, issued a statement denying "any suggestion that the containment structure is on the brink of an accident".
Its chairman Viktor Chebrov said a commission investigating the higher readings had found no proof of a chain reaction. But he stressed a new structure had to be built.
Kostenko said on Tuesday that water seeping through 1,000 square metres of cracks had increased neutron activity and caused the limited nuclear chain reaction.
He said no one knew for certain just what was occurring inside the structure, an engineering feat erected in the chaotic aftermath of the 1986 fire and explosion.
But other officials, supported by Ukraine's most respected academics, backpedalled within 24 hours. Statements were read on evening newscasts saying the high readings were not unusual.

President Leonid Kuchma's top security official, an expert in nuclear rocket technology, said Kostenko was not qualified to make such judgments. Kostenko himself retreated by saying any new reaction would be limited in scale.

Russian nuclear experts also said they saw no danger from the increases. A senior official of Russia's Nuclear Energy Ministry told Interfax news agency that measuring equipment inside the "tomb" was too old to give reliable readings.
Western experts said the levels were far below anything which could provoke a new explosion.
Residents questioned on Kiev streets all appeared resigned to the risks of living within 140 km (90 miles) of the station.
"It does worry me. But this has been going on for so long that we're used to it," said office worker Galina Isakova, 59.
"But what are we supposed to believe with all these statements and denials?"
Wealthy Group of Seven countries have pledged more than $3 billion to help Ukraine meet its pledge to close Chernobyl's two working reactors by the year 2000.
But Kostenko, Ukraine's top negotiator on Chernobyl, and other ministers say the money is not being released quickly enough and say the date may be postponed unless the West proves more forthcoming.
They also accuse the West of concentrating too much on upgrading Ukraine's inefficient energy sector and forgetting the dangers posed by the "sarcophagus".
